analysis.one_liner: Stops medical bills from appearing on credit reports or affecting credit decisions.
analysis.headline: The bill has sat in the Senate Banking Committee since July 2025 with no action taken.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would amend the Fair Credit Reporting Act so that credit bureaus cannot put medical debt on a person's credit report, even bills sent to collections. It would also require the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau to change its rules within a year so that lenders cannot consider medical debt when deciding whether to make a loan. A companion CFPB rule making a similar change for mortgage lending was blocked by a court and vacated, so Congress acting would lock the protection in by statute.
analysis.who_benefits: People who carry medical debt — a group that cuts across party lines and includes many working and middle-income families — would benefit. Removing medical bills from credit reports raises credit scores, which means cheaper mortgages, car loans, and credit cards, and fewer rejections. CFPB research has found medical debt is a poor predictor of whether someone repays a loan, and roughly one in five households carries it.

how_it_helps.text: It changes the Fair Credit Reporting Act so credit bureaus cannot include any medical debt — including debt sent to collections — on consumer reports.
It directs the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau to amend its rules within a year so creditors cannot use medical debt when deciding whether to lend.

analysis.who_pays: Debt collectors and credit bureaus lose a tool they use: collectors often report medical debt to pressure payment, and bureaus sell that data. Lenders lose one piece of information in credit decisions. Lenders argue medical debt indicates higher risk; the CFPB found it predicts repayment poorly, so the practical cost to lenders is limited.

drawbacks.text: Lenders would lose access to medical debt as a signal in credit decisions; the industry argues medical debt can indicate willingness to repay, so removing it could lead lenders to price risk differently.
The bill requires CFPB rulemaking within one year, so its practical effect depends on the Bureau writing and enforcing the implementing regulation on schedule.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real and targeted: millions of people whose credit was damaged by medical bills they often could not control would see scores rise and borrowing costs fall. The cost is modest and mostly falls on collectors and credit bureaus. The main trade-off is that creditors lose one signal that some argue correlates with repayment risk, though research cited in the CFPB's rulemaking found medical bills are poor predictors of repayment and often reflect billing errors or insurance disputes.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Banking Committee after introduction and has sat there with no hearing, markup, or vote.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on July 29, 2025 and read twice, then referred to the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs.
No further action — no committee markup, hearing record, floor vote, or House counterpart action — appears in the bill's action history.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Medical debt collectors and credit bureaus keep their current leverage; borrowers with medical debt gain nothing.

for.name: Sen. Jeff Merkley
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill in the Senate.

for.name: Sens. Blumenthal, Fetterman, Welch, Warnock, and Gillibrand

against.name: Senate Banking Committee leadership
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral, leaving it without a hearing or vote.

against.name: Credit bureaus and medical debt collection industry
against.what_they_did: Have publicly opposed restrictions on reporting and collecting on medical debt.

sides.party_line_note: All six original sponsors are Democrats; no Republican support is recorded.

industries.note: Their tool of reporting unpaid medical bills to credit bureaus to pressure payment would be eliminated, reducing their leverage over patients.
They would no longer include medical debt in reports; they had already voluntarily removed small medical collections, so the added burden is limited.
They could no longer factor medical debt into credit decisions; some argue it is a predictive signal, though the CFPB has found medical debt is a weak predictor of repayment.

analysis.trajectory: With only Democratic sponsorship, no Republican cosponsors, and no action in the Banking Committee for months, the bill is unlikely to advance this Congress unless it is attached to a larger package; bills at this stage typically die quietly at the end of the session.
